questions.question: Explain why the stages of the accounting cycle cannot be done in a different order — use the relationship between the journals and the ledger as your example.
questions.expected_answer: Each stage depends on the output of the previous one. The ledger is posted from journal column totals, so the journals must be completed and totalled first; without journals there is nothing to post, and without ledger balances there is nothing to list in the trial balance.

questions.question: A friend says: 'My trial balance balances, so my books are perfect.' How would you correct their understanding?
questions.expected_answer: A balancing trial balance only proves that total debits equal total credits — arithmetic equality. Errors such as posting the right amount to the wrong account on the correct side, or leaving a transaction out completely, do not disturb the balance, so the books can still contain mistakes.

questions.question: In your own words, describe what each of the six stages of the accounting cycle produces, using a single cash sale as your running example.
questions.expected_answer: The source document (till slip) produces evidence of the sale; the journal (CRJ) produces a classified chronological record; posting produces updated ledger balances in Bank and Sales; the trial balance produces a checked list of balances; the final accounts produce the gross and net profit; the financial statements produce the reports the owner reads.
